Boston University, U.S.A.

Abstract

Temporal isolation is one of the most significant challenges that must be addressed before Multi-Processor Systems-on-Chip (MPSoCs) can be widely adopted in mixed-criticality systems with both time-sensitive real-time (RT) applications and performance-oriented non-real-time (NRT) applications. Specifically, the main memory subsystem is one of the most prevalent causes of interference, performance degradation and loss of isolation. Existing memory bandwidth regulation mechanisms use static, dynamic, or predictive DRAM bandwidth management techniques to restore the execution time of an application under contention as close as possible to the execution time in isolation.

In this paper, we propose a novel distribution-driven regulation whose goal is to achieve a timeliness objective formulated as a constraint on the probability of meeting a certain target execution time for the RT applications. Using existing interconnect-level Performance Monitoring Units (PMU), we can observe the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) of the per-request memory latency. Regulation is then triggered to enforce first-order stochastic dominance with respect to a desired reference. Consequently, it is possible to enforce that the overall observed execution time random variable is dominated by the reference execution time. The mechanism requires no prior information of the contending application and treats the DRAM subsystem as a black box. We provide a full-stack implementation of our mechanism on a Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) platform (Xilinx Ultrascale+ MPSoC), evaluate it using real and synthetic benchmarks, experimentally validate that the timeliness objectives are met for the RT applications, and demonstrate that it is able to provide 2.2x more overall throughput for NRT applications compared to DRAM bandwidth management-based regulation approaches.

L102@P1: II. BACKGROUND
L103@P1: A. Memory & Cache Model
L104@P1: Modern computer systems employ a hierarchical memory
L105@P1: architecture to bridge the performance gap between fast onchip processing elements (PEs) and the slower off-chip main
L106@P1: memory. The hierarchy consists of multiple levels of caches
L107@P1: and the main memory. The cache levels closer to the PE, such
L108@P1: as the L1 cache, are typically private to each PE. The lastlevel cache (LLC) is generally shared among multiple PEs and
L109@P1: directly interfaces with the memory controller. The memory
L110@P1: controller is responsible for the data movement between the
L111@P1: on-chip logic and the off-chip main memory (e.g., DRAM).
L112@P1: Memory bandwidth is the rate at which cache lines are
L113@P1: transferred between the LLC and the main memory. Two
L114@P1: architectural events contribute to the memory activity: cache
L115@P1: refills and write-backs. Upon a refill, a cache line is fetched
L116@P1: from lower to higher levels of the hierarchy. During a writeback, a dirty line being evicted from higher levels is written
L117@P1: back to lower levels, eventually reaching the main memory.
L118@P1: The combined rate of refills and write-backs between the LLC
L197@P2: The feature-rich nature of PS-PL platforms opens a range
L198@P2: of opportunities to rethink memory bandwidth regulation to
L199@P2: overcome traditional challenges of state-of-the-art PMC-based
L200@P2: techniques such as MemGuard and MemPol. Without loss of
L201@P2: generality, all memory bandwidth regulators can be decomposed into three individual modules:
L202@P2: 1) An accounting module whose objective is to obtain and/or
L203@P2: estimate the PEs’ memory activity metrics (e.g., refills,
L204@P2: write-backs).
L205@P2: 2) A decision module whose objective is to decide on what
L206@P2: actions to undertake (i.e., halt, resume, no-action), based
L207@P2: on the current and past memory activity.
L208@P2: 3) An enacting module whose objective is to conduct the
L209@P2: action dictated by decision module.
L210@P2: Realizing each of these modules on an off-the-shelf platform at
L211@P2: the software level comes with technical challenges that hinder
L212@P2: the regulation’s quality. Let us closely examine the models and
L213@P2: limitations of both regulators.
L214@P2: A. MemGuard Model
L215@P2: In a MemGuard-like regulator, as mentioned in Sec. II-B,
L216@P2: the PMC is used as a countdown counter. When its value
L217@P2: reaches zero, an interrupt is issued1immediately to execute
L218@P2: the decision module. Hence, the delay between the moment
L219@P2: throttling is required and its enacting is short, meaning that
L220@P2: MemGuard does not suffer from budget overshooting. A
L221@P2: second periodic interrupt is required to replenish the budget
L222@P2: and enforce a given memory bandwidth value over time. Unfortunately, when higher enforcement granularity is requested,
L223@P2: the reliance on two interrupt handlers becomes problematic.
L224@P2: Achieving finer granularity with the same target bandwidth
L225@P2: implies that both the per-period budget and the replenishment
L226@P2: period must be smaller. Consequently, a ten-fold granularity
L227@P2: increase can lead to a twenty-fold increase in the delivered
L228@P2: interrupt rate. Due to this limitation, MemGuard typically operates at millisecond-granularity. At microsecond-granularity,
L229@P2: it incurs prohibitive overhead [10]. In short, MemGuard is
L230@P2: good at preventing overshooting, but realistically, it can only
L231@P2: operate at millisecond-scale granularity.
L232@P2: B. MemPol Model
L233@P2: Recognizing the overhead problem, MemPol proposes to
L234@P2: use other auxiliary on-chip PE(s) to execute the regulation
L235@P2: logic. Now that the PMC(s) can be sampled from an external
L236@P2: PE and since the regulator also resides outside the core(s)
L237@P2: under regulation, the bandwidth estimation must be done

L246@P2: said approaches for the accounting and enacting modules is
L247@P2: that MemPol no longer injects interrupts in the control flow of
L248@P2: the regulated PEs. With less overhead, MemPol can operate in
L249@P2: microsecond-scale granularity. However, the periodic sampling
L250@P2: nature makes it prone to overshooting problems. Indeed, regulation can only react as fast as the maximum achievable polling
L251@P2: frequency. If a burst of memory transactions occurs, MemPol
L252@P2: cannot respond until the newest PMC reading is polled. In
L253@P2: short, MemPol can operate on microsecond-granularity due to
L254@P2: low overhead but is prone to overshooting problems.
